source.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
source.authors: Jake Ward; P. Riechers; Adam Shai

page_placements.theme: Native neurons exhibit heterogeneous selectivity and mixed signals

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines SAE feature recovery in a reasoning-tuned LLM adapter, a new setting for the claim's indirect-evidence version; it does not test the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The SAE results bear on V4. Benchmark scores and adapter ablations concern reasoning performance, not the claim versions, so they are not rows. The comparison of individual adapter directions with MLP neurons does not test feature superposition or show that features are spread across neurons.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a cross-layer SAE as an interpretability tool on a rank-1 LoRA's 448-dim activation state and reports only how interpretable its features are, using LLM autointerpretation. It never mentions superposition. It reports no reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, sparsity-versus-dimension analysis, or evidence that features outnumber dimensions. A share of features judged monosemantic by gpt-5-mini describes the tool's output, not whether the model stores sparse features in superposition. So no claim version is tested and no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a rank-1 LoRA recovers 73-90% of full-finetune reasoning performance. They find that its individual directions are about as monosemantic as MLP neurons and fire on reasoning-specific tokens. They also find that a cross-layer SAE extracts additional monosemantic features. They caveat that LLM autointerpretation and categorization are subjective and may miss features' true roles.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a trained rank-1 LoRA and a cross-layer SAE on its activations; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method or measure feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors say the SAE feature categorization is subjective and sensitive to prompt wording.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE latents trained on the 448-dim LoRA activation state are judged 'cleanly monosemantic' far more often (62%) than individual LoRA directions (22%), per gpt-5-mini autointerp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary decomposition of a low-dimensional adapter state yields more interpretable units than its basis directions (autointerp-judged).

fits_no_version.finding: Individual rank-1 LoRA directions and base-model MLP neurons have similar autointerp monosemantic and polysemantic shares (Figure 1: about 20-22% monosemantic, about 47-49% polysemantic). No superposition interpretation is offered.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Basis-aligned adapter directions are about as often polysemantic as MLP neurons in Qwen-2.5-32B.

record.problems: Only one model is studied, and the evaluation is mostly on math-related reasoning. Feature interpretations and categories rely heavily on LLM-based autointerpretation and autocategorization; the authors say these can be subjective and prompt-sensitive. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the feature-classification results.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. Reasoning benchmark scores and component ablations are outside the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All: toy-model overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons or recoverable by an SAE. The SAE here gets no fidelity or reconstruction check and no superposition analysis.
All: completeness, stability, canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T3' with V4 'supports' is overturned: the paper makes no superposition claim and gives no SAE fidelity metrics. The Figure 1 MLP-vs-LoRA comparison is not in the rows; it is recorded under fits_no_version. Only one model is studied, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or feature importance.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise without capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE feature extraction from a trained adapter's activation state, not whether features are spread across neurons in ordinary LLM representations or whether the same result holds across models and training settings.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
